query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In as-solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn, the dynamic strength–ductility balance across a range of temperatures and strain rates is primarily governed by a temperature- and strain rate-dependent interaction between partial dislocation slip and stacking fault formation. The absence of Co lowers the stacking fault energy, thereby promoting stacking fault nucleation that both impedes dislocation motion (enhancing strength) and accommodates localized plasticity (preserving ductility).
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled dynamic loading (tension or compression) tests at strain rates ranging from 10^-3 s^-1 to 10^3 s^-1 and temperatures from cryogenic up to 600 K using in-situ high-speed diffraction and TEM imaging.
generation.conditions: Dynamic mechanical tests performed under constant and reproducible strain rates and temperatures with real-time microstructural tracking.
generation.structural_mediator: Evolution of stacking faults and partial dislocation configurations
generation.mechanism: The lower stacking fault energy in Co-free FeNiCrMn enhances the formation of stacking faults during dynamic deformation. These stacking faults act as barriers to dislocation movement, increasing yield strength, while simultaneously providing sites for localized plasticity that sustain ductility. Variation in temperature and strain rate modulates the extent of stacking fault formation and dislocation mobility.
generation.predicted_outcome: In-situ observations will reveal a higher density of stacking faults and a correlated increase in yield strength at lower temperatures and higher strain rates, while still retaining sufficient ductility. Conversely, if stacking fault activity is diminished under these conditions, the expected strain hardening and strength enhancements will not be observed.
generation.baseline: Comparative quasi-static mechanical tests at similar temperatures, where lower dynamic effects on stacking fault formation are expected.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable to as-solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn alloys and may not hold if significant post-solidification annealing, precipitation or compositional variations occur.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between stacking fault density and the mechanical properties across the full range of temperatures and strain rates remains uncertain and may be influenced by additional minor deformation mechanisms.

falsification_experiment.design: Using in-situ high-speed TEM and diffraction techniques, subject as-solidified FeNiCrMn samples to dynamic tensile and compressive loading at strain rates between 10^-3 s^-1 and 10^3 s^-1 across temperatures from cryogenic to 600 K. Track the evolution of stacking faults and measure partial dislocation density concurrently with mechanical properties.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If dynamic tests do not show a consistent correlation between increased stacking fault density (and associated partial dislocation interactions) with enhanced yield strength and maintained ductility, or if another mechanism (such as twinning or phase transformation) dominates the dynamic deformation behavior, then the hypothesis is falsified.

This study focuses on the cobalt-free medium-to-high-entropy alloys AlxCrFe2Ni2 and AlxTixCrFe2Ni2, investigating the influence of Alx and Tix (where x = 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5, and 0.6) on the development of microstructural and mechanical properties in as-cast and annealed states. Structural changes were examined using optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements, while mechanical properties were evaluated through Vickers hardness testing and compression testing. X-ray diffraction analysis of the AlxCrFe2Ni2 alloys confirmed that increasing the Al content in the as-cast state leads to the formation of a BCC phase, which completely dissolves into the FCC matrix after homogenization annealing. These single-phase alloys exhibit good ductility with relatively high strain hardening, such as the Al0.6CrFe2Ni2 alloy, which achieved a maximum compressive strength of σmax=1511 MPa at 50% deformation. decision.trend: Over the past few years, researchers have examined how multi-principal-element alloys respond to high strain rates and varying temperatures, but mostly in Co-containing compositions (e.g., Al0.7CoCrFeNi or CoNiCrFeMn). Early work (PMC6478865) focused on precipitation-strengthened eutectic high-entropy alloys under quasi-static versus dynamic loading, establishing that controlling precipitate structure can boost high-rate strength without losing ductility. Subsequent studies (PMC6488616) measured strain-rate sensitivity and transformation-induced plasticity in various TRIP-enabled high-entropy alloys, showing that phase transformations and stacking-fault-mediated mechanisms are vital to sustaining both strength and ductility at elevated rates. Later atomistic simulations (PMC8398136) on CoNiCrFeMn revealed temperature-dependent superplasticity due to partial dislocation motion, highlighting how high-entropy chemistries incur frictional resistance that can enhance hardening under dynamic loads. While these insights clarify the role of stacking faults, partial dislocations, microstructure, and short-range order in dynamic conditions, none specifically disentangle the unique effects of removing Co from the FeNiCrMn system, leaving the fundamental mechanism that governs its strength–ductility balance under high strain rates and varied temperatures insufficiently resolved.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear whether the dynamic response in Co-free FeNiCrMn is primarily governed by dislocation slip, twinning, or phase transformations, and how these mechanisms depend on temperature and strain rate without Co’s impact on stacking fault energy and short-range order. Prior results in related alloys suggest strong interactions among partial dislocations, faulting, and possible h.c.p. nano-domains, but a clear, experimentally validated mechanistic model for Co-free FeNiCrMn is still missing.
decision.lever: High-speed in-situ diffraction or TEM tracking of dislocation motion, stacking faults, and phase transformations in as-solidified FeNiCrMn across 10^-3 to 10^3 s^-1 strain rates and temperatures from cryogenic to moderate (up to 600 K)
decision.why: Real-time characterization at multiple strain rates and temperatures will reveal whether dislocation slip, twin formation, or local phase transitions control the dynamic ductility and flow stress in Co-free FeNiCrMn. This approach follows from prior dynamic studies on related HEAs (PMC6478865, PMC6488616, PMC8398136). By directly measuring how microstructure evolves under controlled conditions, one can systematically test whether stacking-fault and partial-dislocation interactions, in the absence of Co, drive the observed strength–ductility synergy in FeNiCrMn.
